title: Midnight Sprints and 200 Species: Inside the Teen Birding World Series
summary: It's just after midnight in north New Jersey when a white SUV screeches to a halt beside a deserted park. Three teenage boys burst out and sprint across a field, vault a fence, and crane their necks toward giant nests atop a pole. They're hunting for a sleeping monk parakeet—and after 10 tense minutes, 16-year-old Otys Train yells, "I got it, I got it, I got it!" This is the 43rd annual World Series of Birding, a 24-hour marathon where teams race to identify as many bird species as possible within New Jersey. For Otys, Jack Trojan (17), and Zade Pacetti (16), it's not just a hobby—it's a fierce competition. They call themselves the Pete Dunnelins, a portmanteau of dunlins (a shorebird) and Pete Dunne, the legendary birder who founded the event in 1984. The competition, run by New Jersey Audubon, doubles as a conservation fundraiser and draws 87 teams this year, from first-graders to veterans. The Pete Dunnelins have dominated the high school division, placing first for two years straight. Last year, they tied with their "nemeses," the Flying Penguins, at 199 species. This year, they're gunning for 200. Their preparation is meticulous: a spreadsheet schedules every minute of the day. "Every minute we're driving, we've accounted for," says team captain Jack Trojan. But nature is unpredictable. "Birds are animals, and you can't really predict too well when you're going to see or hear everything." After the parakeet, it's "owl time," then a marshland trail in pitch darkness. Here, Otys's skill shines—he's memorized hundreds of bird calls. He instantly picks out the whinny of a sora, the cheep of a swamp sparrow, and the nasal "peent" of an American woodcock. The teens whisper and confer; competition rules demand unanimous agreement before listing a species. Their dads, serving as drivers and snack-enforcers, watch silently from a distance. "We always used to have a lot of laughing fits," says Jeff Train, Otys's dad, "but no longer." The boys are laser-focused. As dawn approaches, they've already notched dozens of species, but the clock is ticking. For these young birders, it's a test of endurance, knowledge, and teamwork—a thrilling blend of science and sport that turns a quiet marsh into a high-stakes arena.
why_it_matters: The story shows how citizen science and hobbies build real skills—observation, data collection, and teamwork—that matter for future careers in science and conservation, while also proving that passion can turn a quiet marsh into a high-stakes arena.

background_read: The World Series of Birding began in 1984 as a novel way to combine competitive birdwatching with conservation fundraising, run by New Jersey Audubon (a nonprofit dedicated to protecting birds and their habitats).
Birders often contribute valuable data to citizen-science projects like eBird, helping scientists track migration patterns and population changes.
Monk parakeets, which the team spotted at midnight, are not native to North America; they established wild colonies after escaping from captivity and now thrive in some urban areas.
Memorizing bird songs and calls—a skill Otys Train uses—is a hallmark of expert birders, allowing them to identify species hidden in dense vegetation or darkness.
Pete Dunne, who founded the event, is a legendary figure in the birding community and a former director of New Jersey Audubon’s Cape May Bird Observatory, helping popularize the sport.

perspectives.description: The World Series of Birding raises funds for conservation and encourages young people to connect with nature. By turning birdwatching into a sport, it trains a new generation of environmental stewards who can contribute to scientific data collection.

The intense emphasis on winning—minute-by-minute scheduling, unanimous agreement rules—may risk burnout and turn a relaxed hobby into a high-pressure contest. Some birders worry that the competitive format overshadows the simple joy of observing nature.

Competitive birding reflects a broader trend of 'gamifying' citizen science, which can increase public engagement but also raises questions about data quality and whether speed outweighs thoroughness. The event’s long history (since 1984) shows how amateur naturalists have long contributed to ornithology.

If events like this continue to attract teenage participants, we might see more investment in youth outdoor programs and technology that supports real-time species identification. The skills these teens develop—acute listening, teamwork under pressure—will be valuable whether they become scientists or advocates.
